title: (Scenario) You deploy a new version that writes data in a new format, then discover a bug and need to roll back: why can't you simply deploy the old binary (the old code may not understand the new data), and what is the expand-and-contract principle for safe rollback (ensure old and new versions can coexist throughout the migration)?
shortTitle: Why can't you simply deploy the old binary after writing data in a new format, and what is expand-and-contract?
keyPoints: Code reverts instantly on redeploy; data does NOT -- rows written in the new format stay.
The old binary encounters data in a shape it was never programmed to read: crash, wrong results, or silent corruption.
Expand phase: add the new format additively, dual-write both old and new, so either binary can run.
Coexistence phase: run new code but keep producing old format; verify both formats agree; backfill history.
Contract phase (separate, later deploy): stop dual-writing, drop the old format -- the one irreversible step.
During the entire expand-coexist window, rollback is always safe because the old format is maintained.
Expand-and-contract applies to DB schemas, API shapes, event schemas, file formats, and cache layouts.

s1_definition.oneliner: The old binary cannot read data written in a new format, so you keep both formats alive through expand (add new, keep old), coexist, and only contract (remove old) once rollback is no longer needed.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **The trap** -- code reverts instantly; data does not. Rows written in the new format stay after rollback.
- **Expand** -- add the new format additively; dual-write both old and new in one deploy.
- **Coexist** -- run new code but keep producing old format; verify; backfill history in throttled batches.
- **Contract** -- stop dual-writing, drop old format; the one irreversible step, done as a separate, later deploy.
- **Rollback safety** -- during expand and coexist, either binary can run because both formats are maintained.
- **Applies to** -- DB schemas, API shapes, event schemas, file formats, cache layouts.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India switches its ledger to a new format overnight. If a problem appears and they bring back yesterday's clerk, he cannot read a single entry. Expand-and-contract: write every entry in both old and new format for a long period. Either clerk can work. Only after the bank is completely sure do they stop writing the old format.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Expand-and-Contract Timeline

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Deploy 1: EXPAND                              │
  │ - ADD amount_minor column                     │
  │ - Dual-write: amount + amount_minor           │
  │ - Either old or new binary can run ✓          │
  │ - Rollback: SAFE                              │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Coexistence (days/weeks)                      │
  │ - Verify both columns agree                   │
  │ - Backfill old rows                           │
  │ - Build confidence                            │
  │ - Rollback: STILL SAFE                        │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Deploy 2: CONTRACT (separate, later)          │
  │ - Stop dual-writing                           │
  │ - DROP amount column                          │
  │ - Rollback: NO LONGER SAFE ← irreversible     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
When a new version writes data in a new format and you need to roll back, deploying the old binary is not enough because code reverts instantly but data does not. Every row written in the new format stays, and the old binary encounters data it was never programmed to read: crash, wrong results, or silent corruption.

Expand-and-contract makes rollback safe by never having a moment where only one format exists during the risky window. In the expand phase, add the new format additively and dual-write both old and new. During coexistence, verify both formats agree and backfill history. Only in the contract phase, as a separate later deploy, stop dual-writing and drop the old format. Throughout expand and coexist, either binary can run, so rollback is always safe.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj used this to change amount storage from decimal rupees to integer paise. The team dual-wrote both fields, verified agreement, backfilled history, and only dropped the old column weeks later. The same pattern applies to API shapes, event schemas, and cache layouts.

Remember one sentence: the old binary cannot read data written in a new format, so keep both formats alive through expand (add new, keep old) and coexist, and only contract (remove old) once rollback is no longer needed.
